explain.say: An old king decides to split his kingdom between his three daughters, and asks: which of you loves me most? Shakespeare wrote King Lear around 1606. The board shows two families, Lear's on the left and Gloucester's on the right, and the lies that link them.

explain.say: Soon his flattering daughters shut him out. Look at the storm panel. Lear rages on the heath, shouting: Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks! He meets a beggar and sees a poor, bare, forked animal: a human without power. What does Lear learn in the storm?

explain.say: The play mirrors itself. On the left, Lear trusts the wrong children. On the right, Gloucester trusts his lying son Edmund and disowns loyal Edgar. A warning: Gloucester is cruelly blinded on stage. He says that we are to the gods as flies to wanton boys. Why tell the story twice?

explain.say: Lear wakes to Cordelia's forgiveness, but she is hanged and he dies over her body. In 1681 Nahum Tate rewrote it with a happy ending, which held the stage for about 150 years. Brilliant work. Challenge: argue whether Shakespeare's ending is too cruel, or the point.

faq.a: In the love test she refuses to flatter him, saying she loves him according to her duty. Lear, wanting public praise, takes this as coldness and disowns her in a rage.
asks: Why is Lear angry with Cordelia?

faq.q: What happens in the storm scene?
faq.a: Shut out by Goneril and Regan, Lear rages on the heath in a storm with his Fool and Kent, meets Edgar disguised as Poor Tom, and begins to feel for the poor and powerless.

faq.q: What is the subplot of King Lear?
faq.a: The Earl of Gloucester is tricked by his illegitimate son Edmund into disowning his loyal son Edgar. It mirrors Lear's mistake with his daughters.
Regan and Cornwall punish him for helping Lear, after Edmund betrays him. The blinding is the play's most violent scene, and he only sees the truth about his sons once blind.

faq.q: Did King Lear ever have a happy ending?
faq.a: Yes. Nahum Tate's 1681 version let Cordelia live and marry Edgar. It was performed instead of Shakespeare's ending until the nineteenth century.

facts: King Lear was probably written around 1605 to 1606.
It survives in two different texts: the 1608 quarto and the 1623 First Folio.
Nahum Tate's happy-ending version of 1681 replaced Shakespeare's on stage until the 1830s.
